markers.mechanism: Mandarin has no inflectional tense; aspect/time is expressed lexically. Learners drop English -ed and irregular past forms.
markers.prompt_hint: When the sentence has a past-time adverbial (yesterday, last week, ago, in 2020) but a bare verb stem, mark the verb with the correct past tense form.

markers.mechanism: Mandarin plural marker -men is restricted (mostly to human referents) and often dropped after numerals; learners omit English plural -s.
markers.prompt_hint: Add plural -s to count nouns following numerals greater than one (three book→three books, two car→two cars).

markers.mechanism: Mandarin is topic-prominent; learners front the topic regardless of grammatical role.
markers.prompt_hint: When a topicalized object precedes the subject ('This book, I read it'), restructure to canonical SVO order unless the speaker is explicitly emphasizing.

examples.input: Although it rained, but we went.

markers.prompt_hint: Drop the redundant second conjunction in 'Although X, but Y' / 'Because X, so Y' / 'Even though X, still Y' patterns.

markers.mechanism: Mandarin adjectives function as stative verbs and require no copula; learners drop 'is/are' before adjectival predicates.
markers.prompt_hint: Insert 'is/are/am' before predicate adjectives where the speaker dropped the copula.

markers.mechanism: Mandarin wo juede (I feel/think) commonly appears medially or finally; transferred 'I think' lands in non-initial English positions.

examples.input: It is a good idea, I think.
examples.output: I think it is a good idea.

markers.prompt_hint: Move sentence-medial or sentence-final 'I think' / 'I feel' / 'I guess' to the front of the clause.

markers.mechanism: Mandarin dui ('right, correct') is used as acknowledgment without commitment; transferred 'yeah' fills the same role and reads as agreement in English.
markers.prompt_hint: When 'yeah' or 'yes' appears as a standalone backchannel in a written transcript with no clear question to answer, evaluate whether it carries content; if purely acknowledgment, drop it.

markers.mechanism: Mandarin a is a clause-medial particle marking self-correction; transferred 'ah' appears mid-sentence in English.

examples.input: He went ah she went to the store.
examples.output: He went—I mean, she went to the store.

markers.prompt_hint: When 'ah' or 'a' interrupts a clause and the next phrase replaces what came before, render as a self-correction (em-dash + 'I mean,' or just resolve to the corrected form).

markers.mechanism: Mandarin relative clauses precede the head noun (head-final); learners preserve this order in English.
markers.prompt_hint: Move pre-nominal relative clauses to post-nominal position with 'that' / 'which' / 'who' (the I read book → the book that I read).

markers.mechanism: Mandarin spoken pronouns are homophonous: tā = he/she/it. Learners use he/she/it interchangeably in English.
markers.prompt_hint: When a referent's gender is established in the surrounding context, correct mismatched pronouns (sister with 'he' → 'she'; brother with 'she' → 'he').

notes: Mandarin typology: isolating, topic-prominent, no inflectional morphology, head-final relative clauses, paired-conjunction logic. Patterns broadly apply to Cantonese and other Sinitic varieties.
